doc.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Discovering jazz through Art Tatum and early piano teachers
summary: Smith explains jazz reached England via banned records; hearing Tatum's Tea for Two focused him, and three local teachers taught him reading, Bach and Chopin.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: It’s interesting to talk, we have talked with I think one other person who came from England — Jillean Williams actually — and we were getting her take on how jazz was kind of spread from America to other parts, and we wondered if you could tell us how it came to be that you became a jazz musician.

Well, it was disseminated through records of course, and when I was a kid, you couldn’t buy American records for some — I’ll never understand to this day why — but they weren’t allowed. The government after the war distrusted everybody I think and American records were not allowed in. But somehow I got to hear a record by Art Tatum, it’s an absolute classic, “Tea for Two.” And up until then I’d just been listening to everybody and imitating anybody, any piano player. I mean I didn’t know the difference between a classical piano and a jazz piano player. I just tried to play anything, you know. I’d listen all day to the radio and then run in to where the piano was and woodshed all this stuff. And then one day I heard this Art Tatum thing, and it was like suddenly getting
a focus. I felt, you know, if I could play like that, you know. And I spent the last 50 years trying, never succeeded, but—

Yes, of course I did. But you have to understand that the war was still on then and I was the same kind of kid as anybody, I didn’t really want to practice, even though I knew I had some talent even then. But luckily, my mother and father managed to send me to some different ladies, local ladies that, the first one taught me to read and play scales which I thank God for that she did that; the next one got me on to the Bach inventions; and the third one got me into early Chopin. And believe me, I was so lucky that these people were there. Because if you can still play some of those Chopin etudes, you are a pretty good piano player. But anyway, I digress. But later on, the American records managed to be in England. They were pirated in. They appeared, even though it was against the law. And of course all those guys with talent or who liked this kind of music managed to get them. And we all managed to hear these records, and so it was an imitative process. And even at the time I left, and I was 25 when I left, it was still the same thing. The records were coming in just in a dribble so you didn’t really get the whole spectrum. And at that time I thought well it’s pointless me staying around London because it’s all kind of imitative and if I really want to test myself I’ve got to go to New York or one of the centers of jazz. So that’s what we did and we never looked back.
